## The question

[Area with double integral in polar coordinates](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4946235/area-with-double-integral-in-polar-coordinates), asked by [a_i_r](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/843686/a-i-r) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2024-07-15; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Determine the area interior to $y^2=2ax-x^2$ and exterior to $y^2=ax$.
>
> The area in artesian coordinates is $$\int_{0}^{a}\int_{\sqrt{ax}}^{\sqrt{2ax-x^2}} dydx$$. To convert it into polar coordinates with the jacobian $r$,we need to find the limits of $r$ and $\theta$. How to find the limits in our desired region?
>
> [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
>
>   [q-1]: 3KSWHrsl.jpg
>
> I have some confusion about the limits of the angle which the answers confirm to be $45$ and $90$. The way areas are added in polar coordinates is by adding differential sectors of circles or little triangles which I have marked in blue. If the lower limit is $45$,then any small sector will have an unintended area which is not the same as our desired area(which is marked in violet). So don't we have to subtract the areas?
:::

(This answer is essentially the same as @zkutch's; I'm just trying to fill in some details.)

To find the limits of integration in polar coordinates, it helps to convert the equations of the bounding curves.

The first curve has equation 
$$\begin{aligned}
    r^2\sin^2\theta &= 2a r\cos \theta - r^2 \cos^2 \theta
\\\implies r^2\sin^2\theta + r^2 \cos^2 \theta &= 2a r\cos \theta
\\\implies r^2 &= 2ar\cos\theta
\\\implies r &= 2a\cos\theta
\end{aligned}$$
The second curve has equation
$$\begin{aligned}
    r^2 \sin^2\theta &= a r \cos\theta
\\\implies    r &= a \frac{\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta} = a \cot \theta \csc \theta
\end{aligned}$$
(We're ignoring the trivial $r=0$ solutions.)

Where do these curves intersect? Since you have $r$ in terms of $\theta$, set the two expressions of $\theta$ equal to each other:
$$2a \cos\theta = a \frac{\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}
    \implies a\cos\theta(2 \sin^2\theta -1) = 0$$
This is satisfied when $\cos\theta = 0$ or $\sin^2\theta = \frac{1}{2}$.
The first implies $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$ (and $r=0$), and the second implies that $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$ or $\theta = \frac{7\pi}{4}$ (and $r=a\sqrt{2}$). In cartesian coordinates, these points are $(0,0)$ and $(a,\pm a)$. By symmetry, we can restrict to the first quadrant and double the result. This gives us the limits $\frac{\pi}{4} \leq \theta \leq \frac{\pi}{2}$. Therefore the area is
$$2\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2} \int_{a \cot\theta\csc\theta}^{2a\cos\theta} r\,dr\,d\theta = \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{4}{3}\right)a^2$$
([Wolfram Alpha link](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input?i2d=true&i=2Integrate%5BIntegrate%5Br%2C%7Br%2Ca+cot%5C%2840%29%CE%B8%5C%2841%29csc%5C%2840%29%CE%B8%5C%2841%29%2C2a+cos%5C%2840%29%CE%B8%5C%2841%29%7D%5D%2C%7B%CE%B8%2CDivide%5B%CF%80%2C4%5D%2CDivide%5B%CF%80%2C2%5D%7D%5D))

The lower limit of the $\theta$ integral is what prevents us from counting that “unintended area” you shaded in blue. You could write the area as a difference of integrals as in
$$2 \left(\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{2a\cos\theta} r\,dr\,d\theta - \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{a \cot\theta\csc\theta} r\,dr\,d\theta\right)$$
But that evaluates to the same thing. In general, whenever $a < c < b$, then $\int_b^c f(x)\,dx = \int_a^c f(x)\,dx - \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.
